headline: Nor'easter floods the Causeway, strands ferries and cuts power to 9,000
dek: A fast-moving storm pushed the evening high tide over the seawall on Front Street. The Causeway is closed, ferries to Gull Island are suspended and crews expect outages to last into Sunday.
author: Priya Raman
caption: Water over the Front Street seawall at about 7:30 p.m. Saturday. Illustration: Harbor Ledger
body:
A nor'easter that strengthened faster than forecast drove the evening high tide over the Front Street seawall on Saturday, flooding the Causeway, the lower Harbor District and parts of the Fishmarket neighborhood.

The tide gauge at the Coast Guard pier peaked at 11.4 feet at 7:52 p.m., the third-highest reading since record keeping began in 1931 and more than two feet above the forecast issued Friday afternoon.

Merrow Electric said about 9,000 customers had lost power by 9 p.m., most of them south of Water Street. The utility said it would not send crews into flooded streets until the water drops, and warned that some customers could be without power into Sunday evening.

Causeway and ferries

Police closed the Causeway in both directions at 6:15 p.m. after water reached the lane markings near the drawbridge. The Gull Island ferry made its last run at 5:30 p.m. and remains suspended. Island residents who need medical help should call 911; the Coast Guard has a boat on standby.

Where to go

The city opened a warming center at the Merrow High School gym on Highland Avenue at 8 p.m. Pets are allowed. Mayor Teresa Vance asked residents in the evacuation zone to stay off the roads and to move cars to the Highland Avenue garage, which is open free of charge until Monday.

Follow our live updates below for road closures, outage numbers and the morning high tide, which is forecast at 8:14 a.m.

headline: What the 2027 budget means for your street, your taxes and your trash pickup
dek: The council will vote Tuesday on a $412 million budget. Here is where the money goes, what changes for homeowners and renters, and the three fights still to come.
author: Ben Castellano
caption: City Hall on Market Square. Illustration: Harbor Ledger
body:
Port Merrow's proposed budget for 2027 is $412 million, up 3.8 percent from this year. Most of the increase goes to two places: the police and fire pension fund, and the first phase of the Front Street seawall rebuild.

Your property tax bill

The tax rate stays flat at $14.20 per $1,000 of assessed value, but assessments rose an average of 6 percent, so the typical homeowner would pay about $190 more next year.

Trash and recycling

Weekly recycling returns in the Harbor District and Fishmarket, reversing a 2024 cut. Yard waste pickup moves to every other week from April to November.

The fights still to come

Three issues could change the final numbers: a request from the school board for $2.1 million more, a council amendment to fund 12 new firefighters, and whether to borrow or pay cash for the seawall design work.

headline: Council delays vote on Fishmarket rezoning after five hours of testimony
dek: More than 90 people signed up to speak. Most asked the council to slow down a plan that would allow six-story buildings on the old cannery lots.
author: Ben Castellano
body:
The Port Merrow City Council voted 5-2 just before midnight Tuesday to postpone a decision on rezoning the Fishmarket waterfront, after more than five hours of public testimony.

The plan would allow buildings up to six stories on four former cannery lots, with 20 percent of new apartments set aside as affordable. Supporters said the city badly needs housing. Opponents, many of them longtime Fishmarket residents and fishing families, said the plan would push out working waterfront businesses.

Councilmember Rosa Delgado, who represents the neighborhood, asked for 60 more days to negotiate protections for the boatyards and the ice house. The vote is now expected in December.

headline: Gull Island ferry gets a new boat, and a schedule riders have asked for since 2019
dek: The 149-passenger Osprey enters service in November with a 6 a.m. weekday run and a last boat at 11:30 p.m. on weekends.
author: Priya Raman
body:
The state ferry authority will put a new boat on the Gull Island run in November, ending two years of breakdowns and cancelled sailings on the 44-year-old Tern.

The Osprey carries 149 passengers and 18 cars and runs on a hybrid diesel-electric system. With two boats in rotation, the authority will add a 6 a.m. weekday departure for workers and a late Saturday boat that island residents have requested at every public meeting since 2019.

headline: The seawall was built for a sea that no longer exists
dek: Port Merrow's seawall was designed in 1962 for storms that now arrive every few years. Rebuilding it will cost at least $180 million. Who pays is still undecided.
author: Priya Raman
body:
When engineers finished the Front Street seawall in 1962, they designed it to hold back a storm tide that they expected to see once a century. The city has now seen that tide four times since 2012.

Higher water, more often

Sea level at the Coast Guard pier has risen about nine inches since the wall was built, and the rate has roughly doubled since 1990. Each inch makes an ordinary storm more likely to overtop the wall.

The price

A 2025 study put the cost of raising and rebuilding the wall at $180 million to $240 million. Federal grants could cover up to 65 percent, but only if the city commits its share first.

headline: Merrow Shipyard wins Navy repair contract, plans to hire 300
dek: The five-year contract to repair support vessels is the yard's largest since the 1990s. Hiring starts in January, with paid training for welders and pipefitters.
author: Marcus Hale
body:
Merrow Shipyard has won a five-year, $640 million contract to repair and maintain Navy support vessels, the largest award in the yard's 118-year history, the company announced Tuesday.

The yard plans to hire about 300 workers over two years, including 120 apprentices. Merrow Community College will run a paid 16-week welding course starting in January, with a job interview guaranteed to everyone who finishes.

headline: Rents on the waterfront rose 11 percent in a year. Wages rose 3.
dek: A Ledger analysis of 2,800 listings shows the gap between what renters earn and what they pay is widest in the Harbor District and Fishmarket.
author: Marcus Hale
body:
The median asking rent for a two-bedroom apartment in Port Merrow reached $2,140 in August, up 11 percent from a year earlier, according to a Ledger analysis of 2,800 rental listings.

Over the same period, average weekly wages in the county rose about 3 percent. A household now needs to earn about $85,600 a year to rent a typical two-bedroom without spending more than 30 percent of its income.

headline: Main Street's last hardware store will close after 81 years
dek: Brannigan's Hardware sold nails by the pound and lent out ladders for free. The owners say they could not find a buyer.
author: Marcus Hale
body:
For 81 years, Brannigan's Hardware has sold nails by the pound, cut keys while you wait and lent ladders to anyone who promised to bring them back.

On Oct. 31, the store will close. Owners Tom and Ellen Brannigan, both in their seventies, spent two years looking for a buyer. 'Everyone loves the store,' Ellen said. 'Nobody wants to run it.'

headline: School board weighs later start times for Merrow High
dek: Moving the first bell from 7:25 to 8:30 would cost about $600,000 a year in extra buses. Students packed the meeting to support it.
author: June Whitaker
body:
Port Merrow's school board heard more than two hours of comment Wednesday on a proposal to move Merrow High's start time from 7:25 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. beginning next fall.

Most of the 40 speakers were students, who cited research on teenage sleep. District staff said the change would require four more buses, costing about $600,000 a year. The board will vote in November.

headline: A reading tutor in every second-grade classroom: how one program is working
dek: Two years in, second-graders in the program are reading at grade level at nearly twice the rate of their peers. Teachers say the volunteers are the reason.
author: June Whitaker
body:
Every weekday at 9 a.m., 64 volunteers walk into second-grade classrooms across Port Merrow and sit down with a child and a book.

The Read Merrow program, now in its third year, pairs each tutor with three students for 20 minutes a day. District data shows 58 percent of participating students were reading at grade level by spring, compared with 31 percent two years earlier.

headline: Gulls clinch first playoff berth since 2011 with walk-off in the ninth
dek: Rookie catcher Eli Navarro's two-run single sent 6,100 fans home happy and the Gulls into the league semifinals.
author: Diego Ferreira
body:
Rookie catcher Eli Navarro lined a two-run single into the right-field corner with two outs in the ninth inning Sunday, and the Port Merrow Gulls beat the Lowell Hawks 5-4 to clinch their first playoff berth in 15 years.

A sellout crowd of 6,100 at Harbor Park stayed on its feet for the final inning. The Gulls open the semifinal series at home on Friday.

headline: Merrow High runs past Bayside, stays unbeaten
dek: Senior Tavon Price ran for 212 yards and three touchdowns as the Mariners improved to 5-0.
author: Diego Ferreira
body:
Senior running back Tavon Price ran for 212 yards and three touchdowns Friday night, and Merrow High beat Bayside 35-14 to stay unbeaten.

The Mariners have outscored opponents 171-48 this season. They host rival Northfield on Friday in a game that will likely decide the league title.

headline: The boardwalk chowder ranking, settled at last
dek: We ate 14 bowls in three days so you don't have to. One stand won by a mile, and it isn't the one with the line.
author: Lena Sorensen
body:
There are 14 places on the Port Merrow boardwalk that sell clam chowder, and over three days in September, we ate a bowl at every one of them.

The winner, by unanimous decision of our three tasters, was Dot's, a six-stool counter at the north end that has used the same recipe since 1971. The broth is thin, briny and peppery, the clams are chopped by hand, and there is no flour in it at all.

headline: Harbor Lights festival returns with a new night market on the pier
dek: The three-night festival in late October adds 40 food and craft vendors, a lantern parade and a free shuttle from Highland Avenue.
author: Lena Sorensen
body:
The Harbor Lights festival returns Oct. 23 to 25 with a new night market on the City Pier, a lantern parade along Front Street and a free shuttle from the Highland Avenue garage.

Organizers said 40 vendors will take part, more than half of them from Port Merrow. The festival is free; the lantern-making workshops cost $5.

headline: The Rialto reopens: inside the restoration of Port Merrow's oldest theater
dek: Seven years and $14 million later, the 1916 movie palace has its gold ceiling back, plus an elevator, new seats and a second screen in the old ballroom.
author: Lena Sorensen
body:
The ceiling took two years. Restorers rebuilt more than 3,000 plaster rosettes by hand, then covered them in 23-karat gold leaf, one square at a time.

The Rialto Theatre, which opened on Water Street in 1916 and closed in 2017, reopens Oct. 9 with a screening of the 1924 silent film that played on its tenth anniversary, accompanied by the restored Wurlitzer organ.

headline: The seawall can't wait for a perfect plan
dek: The council should commit the city's share of the seawall design money in Tuesday's budget vote. Every year of delay makes the work more expensive and the next storm more dangerous.
author: Ledger Editorial Board
body:
For a decade, Port Merrow has studied its seawall. We know it is too low. We know the sea is rising. We know a federal program will pay most of the cost of a new one, but only if the city commits its share first.

On Tuesday, the council can do that. The budget includes $9 million to finish the seawall design, and some councilmembers want to delay it another year while they look for cheaper options.

We understand the impulse, but there is no cheaper option. The cost estimate has risen 30 percent since 2022. Commit the money on Tuesday.

headline: Letters: the Fishmarket rezoning, school start times and the ferry
dek: Readers on housing versus the working waterfront, why teenagers need more sleep, and a thank-you to a ferry deckhand.
author: Ledger Editorial Board
body:
Housing and boatyards can share a waterfront. I have lived in the Fishmarket for 40 years. We need apartments for our children, but not at the cost of the boatyards. Give the council its 60 days. Marguerite Silva, Fishmarket

Let them sleep. As a pediatrician, I see the effect of 6 a.m. alarms on teenagers every week. An 8:30 start is worth the buses. Dr. Alan Choi, Highland

Letters may be edited for length and clarity. Send yours to letters@harborledger.example, with your name and neighborhood.

headline: Fishing fleet's scallop season opens with the best prices in a decade
dek: Dock prices topped $19 a pound on opening day. Captains warn that fuel and insurance costs eat most of the gain.
author: Priya Raman
body:
Port Merrow's scallop boats returned on opening day with the highest dock prices in a decade, as low catches up and down the coast pushed buyers to pay more than $19 a pound.

But captains said record prices don't mean record profits. Diesel is up 22 percent over two years, and insurance on a 70-foot boat now runs about $60,000 a year.

headline: A new solar array will power the water treatment plant
dek: The 4-megawatt array on the old landfill should cut the plant's electric bill in half, saving about $700,000 a year.
author: Ben Castellano
body:
The city will build a 4-megawatt solar array on the capped North Point landfill to power the water treatment plant next door, after the council approved a 25-year agreement Tuesday.

Public works director Sam Oduya said the array would supply about 55 percent of the plant's electricity and save about $700,000 a year once it is running in 2028.

headline: How we cover storms, and how you can help
dek: When a storm hits, our coverage is free for everyone, our live updates are timestamped and corrected in public, and your photos and tips go straight to an editor.
author: Nadia Okonkwo
body:
When a storm threatens Port Merrow, our storm coverage is free, like everything we publish, and we put everything we know in one place: a live updates page at the top of our home page, marked with a red banner.

Every update is timestamped. When we get something wrong, we correct it in the live feed and say so, rather than quietly editing the post.

If you see flooding, downed lines or a road closure, send a photo and the location to tips@harborledger.example. An editor reads every message during a storm.
